name: Facet
text: Build the Excava interface in Figma as a clickable prototype first. It lets users *feel* the flow before any code exists, exposing UX flaws early when they’re cheap to fix. The trade-off is that this delays the "real speed" proof until we move to live HTML/CSS, but clarity beats speed in early discovery.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Figma’s polished demo still risks users mistaking the prototype for the real interface, hiding real speed gaps until we hit live HTML/CSS. A better alternative is to prototype only the risky flows in low-fidelity wireframes—then measure actual screentime against those flows to settle the argument.

name: Facet
text:
We should build a low-fidelity wireframe prototype of Excava's riskiest flows to test usability and identify potential speed gaps early on. This approach lets us prioritize and fix the most critical issues before investing in high-fidelity design or live coding, which saves time and resources in the long run. The trade-off is that we'll delay seeing the full visual polish of the interface, but this approach ensures we're solving the right problems first. By focusing on the riskiest flows, we can measure actual screentime and make data-driven decisions to optimize the interface for real speed and usability.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Low-fidelity wireframes hide the *visual* cues that make interfaces feel fast—users won’t perceive lag the same way they do in a polished Figma prototype, so we’ll still miss the real speed gaps until we hit live HTML/CSS. The better alternative is to prototype the risky flows in a *medium-fidelity* interactive mockup (e.g., Figma with basic transitions) to balance realism and early feedback—then measure actual screentime against those flows to settle the argument.

name: Lumen
text:
DECISION: Build a medium-fidelity HTML/CSS demo of Excava’s riskiest flows—live, not polished—then measure real screentime to expose speed gaps before any high-fidelity work.

Result: A working demo that users can *feel* the speed of, with data on where it lags. Owned by the visualization lead.
